timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: If I put my data in AWS, isn't Amazon responsible for keeping it secure?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: That's the number one cloud misconception, Peter. AWS follows the shared responsibility model. They secure the infrastructure - the physical data centers, the hypervisors, the network. You secure everything else - your data, your configurations, your access controls.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So if I mess up a setting, it's on me?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Completely on you. 95% of cloud breaches are customer misconfiguration. Capital One lost 100 million records because of an overly permissive IAM role on an EC2 instance combined with a misconfigured WAF.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: IAM is the crown jewel of cloud security. Never use root accounts. Create IAM roles with least privilege. Use condition keys to restrict access by IP, time, or MFA status. And enable CloudTrail for auditing every API call.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What about S3 buckets? I hear about those getting hacked all the time.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: S3 is the most common source of cloud data leaks. Default settings allow public access. Use S3 Block Public Access at the account level. Enable server-side encryption with KMS. And use S3 access logs to monitor who's accessing what.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Security groups and NACLs provide network-level controls. Security groups are stateful firewalls for instances. NACLs are stateless firewalls for subnets. Use both for defense in depth.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What tools help with all this?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: AWS Security Hub gives you a centralized view. GuardDuty detects threats using ML. Config tracks configuration changes. CloudFormation lets you define infrastructure as code, so you can version-control your security settings.
